standard_text: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers from 1 to 100, with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor.

progression.narrative: 6.NS.6 asks students to do three related things with whole numbers: find the greatest common factor (GCF) of two numbers up to 100, find the least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers up to 12, and use the distributive property to rewrite a sum like 8 + 20 as 4(2 + 5). All three sit on one prerequisite: knowing what factors and multiples ARE and being able to produce them quickly. The progression starts by handing students the lists (S1 and S2) -- with the factors or multiples already written out, the only new work is choosing the greatest COMMON factor or the least COMMON multiple, which is exactly where the classic GCF-vs-LCM swap first shows up. Then the scaffolding comes away: students generate the lists themselves for any pair up to 100 (S3, GCF) or up to 12 (S4, LCM). With GCF secure, the distributive property step (S5) puts it to work: pull the GCF out of both addends and write the sum as a multiple of a sum -- the standard's most test-visible move, and the one where students most often factor one addend and forget the other. Finally S6 sends both ideas into real-world problems, where nobody says 'GCF' or 'LCM' and the student must decide which tool the story is asking for.

steps.rationale: With the factor lists handed to the student, the only new demand is 'greatest AND common' -- isolating the selection step before asking students to generate factors themselves.
The mirror step for multiples: with lists given, students learn that LCM means the FIRST number both lists share, not the biggest and not the product.
Remove the scaffold: generate both factor lists yourself for any pair up to 100, then select the GCF. This is the standard's first full grade-level demand.
Generate multiples yourself for any pair up to 12 and stop at the first common one. Pairs with 7, 8, and 12 expose the shortcut error of just multiplying the two numbers.
Put GCF to work: rewrite a sum of two numbers as GCF x (sum of two numbers with no common factor). This is the distributive property demand of the standard, and it requires factoring BOTH addends.
The extension: real-world problems where the story, not the question, tells you whether to split things into equal groups (GCF) or wait for events to line up (LCM).

skills.name: Recall multiplication facts and factor pairs quickly

prerequisite_skill.description: Fluent recall of multiplication and division facts through 12 x 12
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is 6 x 7? What number times 8 gives 56?

skills.i_do_script: Every skill in this standard leans on fast facts. Watch me find a missing factor: 6 x __ = 42. I ask 'six times WHAT is 42?' and skip-count if I need to: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42 -- that's seven sixes, so the missing factor is 7. Don't lecture; just fire quick facts at the student and let them build speed.

canonical_error.pattern: Recalls a nearby fact instead of the right one, or can't run a fact backward (missing factor)
canonical_error.example: For 6 x __ = 42, the student answers 8 because they remember '48' living near the 6s row
canonical_error.why: The facts were memorized one-directionally (6 x 7 = 42) and never practiced as 'what times 6 gives 42?', so division-shaped recall pulls the nearest familiar product.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- let's check that fact.
redirect_script.prompt: Skip-count by 6 out loud with me: 6, 12, 18... stop when you hit 42. Count how many sixes that took on your fingers.
redirect_script.praise: You ran the fact backward -- that's exactly what factoring is.

skills.item_template: A single multiplication fact, missing-factor fact, is-it-a-factor yes/no, or list-all-factors prompt. Short answer, no choices -- built for timed fluency sprints.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Students weak on the 6s and 7s facts guess 6 or 8
Confusing 56 with 54 (6 x 9) is the common slip
Students who skip-count may land on 6 (54) or 8 (72)
Guessing 7 gives 84; the 12s facts past 10 are shaky
Students who stop at the 10s facts answer 'none'

sample_items.stem: What is 7 x 8?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 54 (from 6 x 9) is the classic near-miss

sample_items.stem: What is 6 x 12?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 60 (6 x 10) plus a guess; the 12s row is the gap

sample_items.stem: Is 4 a factor of 30? (yes or no)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students say yes because 30 is even, like 4

sample_items.stem: Is 6 a factor of 54? (yes or no)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students say no because 54 is not in the 6s row they memorized (6 x 9 = 54)

sample_items.stem: Is 3 a factor of 51? (yes or no)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students say no because 51 looks prime; 5 + 1 = 6 shows it is divisible by 3

sample_items.stem: Is 8 a factor of 60? (yes or no)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students say yes because 60 is divisible by lots of numbers; 60 / 8 = 7.5

sample_items.stem: List all the factors of 10.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students forget 1 and the number itself are factors

sample_items.stem: List all the factors of 16.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students miss 4 x 4 = 16 and skip a factor, or forget 1 and 16

sample_items.stem: List all the factors of 21.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students say 21 is prime because it is odd; 3 x 7 = 21

vocabulary.definition: A whole number that divides another number evenly, with nothing left over.
Two numbers that multiply to make a target number, like 4 and 6 for 24.
The answer you get when you multiply two numbers.

next_steps.if_fail: Review multiplication facts with skip-counting and a facts chart before returning.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 6 x __ = 42.
Read it with me: six times WHAT equals 42. What is this question asking you to find?
If you don't know it cold, how could skip-counting by 6 get you there?
Skip-count together, raising one finger per six: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42.
How many fingers are up? So six times what is 42?
If the student answers 8, they grabbed the nearby fact 6 x 8 = 48. Have them multiply 6 x 8 out loud and compare to 42.
6 x 7 = 42 and 42 / 6 = 7 are the same fact wearing two outfits. Knowing facts backward is what makes factors fast.
Your turn, rapid fire: 8 x __ = 56. Then: is 4 a factor of 30?

skills.name: Distinguish factors of a number from multiples of a number

prerequisite_skill.description: Find factor pairs for whole numbers to 100 and recognize multiples (4.CA.4)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Name one factor of 12 and one multiple of 12. How are they different?

skills.i_do_script: Factors and multiples get swapped constantly, so we pin them down with one picture. Take 6. Factors of 6 fit INSIDE it: 1, 2, 3, 6 -- they divide 6 evenly, and the list stops at 6. Multiples of 6 grow FROM it: 6, 12, 18, 24, ... -- the 6s skip-counting row, and it never ends. Factors are small and few; multiples are big and endless.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses 'factor' and 'multiple' interchangeably -- calls 12 a factor of 6, or 3 a multiple of 6
canonical_error.example: Asked for a factor of 6, the student says 12 'because 6 goes into 12'
canonical_error.why: Both words live in the same multiplication fact (3 x 2 = 6), and the student never anchored which side of the fact each word names: factors divide INTO the number, multiples are what the number builds.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- which direction does that word point?
redirect_script.prompt: Say the sentence both ways and pick the true one: '12 divides evenly into 6' or '6 divides evenly into 12.' Factors of 6 must divide INTO 6. Is 12 smaller than or equal to 6?
redirect_script.praise: You checked which number divides into which -- that's the whole distinction.

skills.item_template: Given a number, identify whether a second number is a factor of it or a multiple of it, or pick the factor/multiple from a short list. MC or short answer.

sample_items.stem: Which number is a FACTOR of 8: 4 or 16?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 16 tempts students who reason '8 goes into 16' -- that makes 16 a multiple, not a factor

sample_items.stem: Which number is a MULTIPLE of 6: 3 or 18?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3 tempts students because 3 is related to 6; but 3 is a factor of 6, not a multiple

sample_items.stem: Is 5 a factor of 20, a multiple of 20, or both?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who blur the words pick 'both'; 5 divides into 20 but 5 is not in the 20s skip-count row

sample_items.stem: Is 30 a factor of 10 or a multiple of 10?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who ignore size say factor; a factor of 10 can never be bigger than 10

sample_items.stem: List the factors of 12, then list the first three multiples of 12.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who swap the words write 12, 24, 36 as 'factors'; watch for missing 1 and 12 in the factor list

sample_items.stem: True or false: every number is both a factor of itself and a multiple of itself.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students say false because they think factors must be smaller and multiples must be bigger

sample_items.stem: Which list shows MULTIPLES of 9: (1, 3, 9) or (9, 18, 27)?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1, 3, 9 is the factor list -- students who pick it are reading 'multiple' as 'factor'

sample_items.stem: Can a factor of 40 be greater than 40? Explain in one sentence.
sample_items.answer: No -- a factor must divide evenly into 40, so it cannot be bigger than 40.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who say yes are picturing multiples, which do grow past 40

sample_items.stem: 7 x 4 = 28. In this fact, which numbers are factors, and what is 28 called?
sample_items.answer: 7 and 4 are factors; 28 is the product (a multiple of both 7 and 4).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students may call 28 a factor because it sits in the same fact family

vocabulary.definition: A number that divides evenly into another number: 4 is a factor of 12.
A number you land on when skip-counting: 12, 24, 36 are multiples of 12.
A number is divisible by another if it divides with no remainder.

worked_example_script.text: Write '6' in the middle of the board. On the left write 'Factors of 6', on the right write 'Multiples of 6'.
What numbers divide evenly into 6 with nothing left over? Let's list them on the left.
Make sure 1 and 6 both make the list -- students routinely leave them off.
Now skip-count by 6 for the right side: 6, 12, 18... How long could this list go?
Look at both lists. Which list has small numbers that stop? Which has big numbers that never stop?
Factors fit INSIDE the number -- few and small. Multiples grow FROM the number -- endless. That size test will save you every time.
Quick check: is 12 a factor of 6 or a multiple of 6? Use the size test to defend your answer.
Last one on your own: name two factors of 20 and two multiples of 20.

skills.name: Identify the greatest common factor from given factor lists
skills.i_do_script: The factor lists are already written for us -- our whole job is finding the biggest number that lives in BOTH lists. Look at 12 and 30 with me. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. I circle every number in both lists: 1, 2, 3, 6. The greatest one circled is 6 -- that's the GCF. Not 30, even though 30 is the biggest number on the board.

canonical_error.pattern: Picks the greatest number visible in the lists instead of the greatest number COMMON to both lists
canonical_error.example: Given the factors of 12 and 30, the student answers 30 because it is the biggest number in the table
canonical_error.why: The student processes 'greatest' but drops 'common' -- they scan for the maximum value instead of first filtering to numbers that appear in BOTH lists, then taking the max of those.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- is that number in BOTH lists?
redirect_script.prompt: Circle every number that appears in the top list AND the bottom list. Only circled numbers can win. Now which circled number is greatest?
redirect_script.praise: You filtered to common first, then picked the greatest -- perfect order.

skills.item_template: A table lists all factors of two whole numbers (pairs <= 50). Student identifies the GCF. MC with 4 choices: smaller common factors, the LCM or a list maximum as distractors. Rendered with a data_table figure.

sample_items.stem: The factors of 12 and 30 are listed in the table. What is the greatest common factor of 12 and 30?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1, 2, and 3 are common factors but not the greatest -- students stop at the first common number they spot

sample_items.stem: The factors of 18 and 24 are listed in the table. What is the greatest common factor of 18 and 24?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 and 3 are smaller common factors; 72 is the LCM -- the GCF-vs-LCM swap

sample_items.stem: The factors of 16 and 20 are listed in the table. What is the greatest common factor of 16 and 20?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 is a smaller common factor; 20 is the biggest number visible in one list; 80 is the LCM

sample_items.stem: The factors of 15 and 25 are listed in the table. What is the greatest common factor of 15 and 25?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 is common but not greatest; 25 is the maximum visible number; 75 is the LCM

vocabulary.definition: A number that divides evenly into another number.
A number that is a factor of BOTH numbers -- it appears in both lists.
The biggest number that is a factor of both numbers, often written GCF.

worked_example_script.text: Draw the table: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30.
The question asks for the greatest COMMON factor. What does 'common' mean when we're looking at two lists?
Go number by number in the top list. Is 1 also in the bottom list? Is 2? Keep going and circle every match.
Watch for the student circling 30 or 15 -- numbers in only ONE list. If it happens, ask: 'Show me that number in the other list.'
Read me just the circled numbers. Which of THOSE is the greatest?
The GCF of 12 and 30 is 6. Notice it is NOT the biggest number in the table -- 'common' filters first, 'greatest' picks second.
Why can't 30 be the answer, even though it's the largest factor listed?
Try one alone: factors of 16 and 20 are on your sheet. Circle the common ones, then name the GCF.

practice_problems.stem: The factors of 8 are 1, 2, 4, 8. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. List every COMMON factor.
The factors of 9 are 1, 3, 9. The factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3, 6. What is the greatest common factor?
The factors of 20 and 28 are listed in the table. What is the GCF of 20 and 28?
practice_problems.notes: Expect some students to answer 28 (biggest visible) or 2 (first common they find).

practice_problems.stem: The factors of 24 and 40 are listed in the table. What is the GCF of 24 and 40?
Ava used the table to find the GCF of 12 and 18. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Ava: 'The greatest number I see is 18, so the GCF is 18.'
practice_problems.answer: GCF = 6. Ava picked the greatest number in the lists, but 18 is not in the factors of 12. The common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, and the greatest of those is 6.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error -- 'greatest' without 'common.'

practice_problems.stem: The factors of 30 and 45 are listed in the table. What is the GCF of 30 and 45?
Two numbers have a GCF of 6. Neither number is 6 or 12. Give a possible pair and list each number's factors to prove it.
practice_problems.answer: Example: 18 and 30. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. Common: 1, 2, 3, 6 -- greatest is 6.
practice_problems.notes: Producing a pair, not just selecting, shows ownership.

practice_problems.stem: The GCF of 16 and a mystery number is 8. The mystery number is between 20 and 30. What is it, and how do you know?
practice_problems.answer: 24. It must be a multiple of 8 between 20 and 30, so 24; and GCF(16, 24) = 8, not 16, because 16 does not divide 24.
practice_problems.notes: Reverses the direction -- from GCF back to the number.

activities.title: Common or Not?
materials: Number cards for the factors of 24 and 36
Two hula-hoop circles or drawn loops (overlapping)
activities.instructions:
1. Label one loop 'Factors of 24' and the other 'Factors of 36'; overlap them in the middle.
2. Partners take turns placing each card: left loop only, right loop only, or the overlap.
3. When all cards are placed, ask: which card in the OVERLAP is greatest? That's the GCF.
4. Debrief: why can't a card outside the overlap ever be the GCF?

activities.title: Fix Ava's GCF
activities.instructions:
1. Students read Ava's work silently and underline the exact sentence where it goes wrong.
2. They rewrite the solution correctly: circle common factors first, then choose the greatest.
3. Debrief question: which word did Ava ignore -- 'greatest' or 'common'?

content.worked_problem: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Ava says: 'The greatest number I see is 18, so the GCF of 12 and 18 is 18.'
content.error_step: Ava picked the greatest number anywhere in the table instead of the greatest number in BOTH lists.
content.why: 18 is not a factor of 12 -- it only appears in one list. The common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, so the GCF is 6.

strategy_links.why: The 'biggest number I see' error is easy to bait and satisfying to find-and-fix from a printed table.
Whiteboard Pass with a factor table shows instantly who is circling numbers from only one list.
Choral response on 'common first, greatest second' cements the two-step order.

questioning_prompts: Before you answer: which numbers appear in BOTH lists? Read them to me.
The word 'greatest' comes with a partner word. What is it, and what does it make you do first?
Could the GCF of two numbers ever be bigger than the smaller number? Why not?
You circled 6. Prove it belongs in both lists.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student names the largest number visible in the table (like 30) as the GCF.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle every number that appears in the top list AND the bottom list. Only circled numbers can win. Now which circled number is greatest?
misconception_redirects.praise: You filtered to common first, then picked the greatest -- perfect order.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student stops at the first common factor they notice (answers 2 or 3) without scanning the whole overlap.
misconception_redirects.say: You found A common factor -- the question wants the GREATEST one. Keep scanning to the end of both lists before you commit.
misconception_redirects.praise: Now you checked the whole list before choosing -- that's how you catch the big one.

quick_checks.prompt: Factors of 10: 1, 2, 5, 10. Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. GCF -- go.
quick_checks.look_for: 5, fast. An answer of 15 means 'greatest without common' is still live; 1 means they stopped at the first match.

quick_checks.prompt: Point to the GCF's home: is it in one list, the other list, or both?
quick_checks.look_for: 'Both' immediately. Hesitation signals the word 'common' hasn't anchored.

worked_solution.stem: The factors of 12 and 30 are listed. What is the greatest common factor of 12 and 30?

steps.annotation: Both lists are given -- our job is only to compare them.
Circle every number that appears in BOTH lists. 'Common' filters first.
Now 'greatest' picks from the circled numbers only -- not from the whole table.
Check: 12 / 6 = 2 and 30 / 6 = 5, both divide evenly.

faded_example.stem: The factors of 18 and 24 are listed. What is the GCF of 18 and 24?

steps.annotation: The lists are given -- read them carefully.
Circle only the numbers that appear in BOTH lists.
Pick the greatest of the circled numbers -- not the greatest number in the table.

sentence_starters: The common factors are ___, so the greatest one is ___.
___ can't be the GCF because it is only in ___ list.

skills.name: Identify the least common multiple from given multiples lists
skills.i_do_script: Now the lists show multiples, and we want the FIRST number both lists share. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, ... Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, ... I run my finger down the 9s list -- the slower list -- and check each one against the 5s: 9? no. 18? no. 27? no. 36? no. 45? YES. The least common multiple of 5 and 9 is 45. Least means first shared, not smallest number.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses LCM with GCF -- picks the greatest common FACTOR (or just a small shared-looking number) instead of the first shared multiple
canonical_error.example: Asked for the LCM of 6 and 8 with both multiples lists showing, the student answers 2 'because 2 goes into both'
canonical_error.why: GCF and LCM are taught side by side and both start with 'common,' so the student reaches for whichever routine surfaces first. They haven't anchored that multiples GROW from the numbers, so the LCM must be at least as big as the larger number.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- is that number IN either multiples list?
redirect_script.prompt: Put your finger on your answer. Find it in the multiples of 6 list. Now find it in the multiples of 8 list. A least common MULTIPLE must sit in both lists -- and it can never be smaller than the bigger starting number.
redirect_script.praise: You found the first number both lists share -- that's exactly what least common multiple means.

skills.item_template: A table lists the first several multiples of two whole numbers (pairs <= 12). Student identifies the LCM. MC with 4 choices: the GCF (swap bait), the product, and a later common multiple as distractors. Rendered with a data_table figure.

sample_items.stem: Some multiples of 5 and 9 are listed in the table. What is the least common multiple of 5 and 9?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5 and 9 are the numbers themselves (and their only common factor is 1, tempting the smallest visible); 60 is a multiple of 5 but not of 9

sample_items.stem: Some multiples of 4 and 6 are listed in the table. What is the least common multiple of 4 and 6?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 is the GCF -- the classic GCF-vs-LCM swap; 24 is the product (and a later common multiple); 36 is also common but not least

sample_items.stem: Some multiples of 8 and 10 are listed in the table. What is the least common multiple of 8 and 10?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 is the GCF (swap); 20 is a multiple of 10 but not of 8; 80 is the product -- a common multiple but not the least

sample_items.stem: Some multiples of 6 and 9 are listed in the table. What is the least common multiple of 6 and 9?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3 is the GCF (swap); 36 and 54 are common multiples that appear later in the lists

vocabulary.definition: A number you land on when skip-counting by a number: 12, 24, 36 are multiples of 12.
A number that appears in BOTH skip-counting lists.
The first (smallest) number both lists share, often written LCM.

worked_example_script.text: Write two rows: Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45. Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45.
We want the LEAST common multiple. In your own words, what are we hunting for in these two rows?
Which row grows faster? Why is it smarter to walk down the 9s row and check each one against the 5s?
Walk the 9s row with your finger: 9 -- in the 5s row? No. 18? No. 27? No. 36? No. 45? Yes!
So what is the LCM of 5 and 9? Point to it in BOTH rows.
If the student says 1 or 5 or another small number, they've slipped into factor-thinking. Ask: 'Is that number in the multiples of 9 row? Multiples grow -- can our answer be smaller than 9?'
Least common multiple means the FIRST number both skip-counting rows share. It will always be at least as big as the bigger number -- here, at least 9.
Your turn: multiples of 4 and 6 are on your sheet. Walk the 6s row and tell me the LCM.

practice_problems.stem: List the first five multiples of 4.
Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20. What is the LCM of 3 and 5?
Some multiples of 6 and 10 are listed in the table. What is the LCM of 6 and 10?
practice_problems.notes: Expect 60 (the product) and 2 (the GCF swap) as wrong answers.

practice_problems.stem: Some multiples of 4 and 10 are listed in the table. What is the LCM of 4 and 10?
Marcus was asked for the least common multiple of 6 and 8. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Marcus: 'The common numbers are 1 and 2, so the LCM of 6 and 8 is 2.'
practice_problems.answer: LCM = 24. Marcus listed FACTORS and found the greatest common factor's territory. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, ... Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, ... The first shared multiple is 24. An LCM can never be smaller than the bigger number.
practice_problems.notes: The GCF-vs-LCM swap, baited directly.

practice_problems.stem: Some multiples of 5 and 6 are listed in the table. What is the LCM of 5 and 6?
The LCM of 4 and a mystery number is 12, and the mystery number is NOT 12. What could the mystery number be? Find both possibilities.
practice_problems.notes: Reverses direction -- from the LCM back to the pair.

practice_problems.stem: Sometimes the LCM of two numbers is just the bigger number. When does that happen? Give an example pair and explain.
practice_problems.answer: When the smaller number is a factor of the bigger one. Example: LCM(4, 12) = 12 because 12 is already a multiple of 4.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch; connects factors and multiples.

activities.title: Skip-Count Showdown
activities.instructions:
1. Flip a pair card. Partner A skip-counts the first number out loud while writing the row; Partner B does the second number at the same time.
2. The FIRST partner to spot a number sitting in both rows circles it and calls 'LCM!'
3. Verify together: is it really in both rows? Is there an earlier shared number?
4. Debrief: why is the LCM never smaller than the bigger number on the card?

activities.title: GCF or LCM? Sort the Answers
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the question cards and answer cards face up.
2. Match each question to its answer -- but the decoy answers are each pair's OTHER value (the GCF when the question wants the LCM).
3. For every match, the group must say which list they imagined: factors (stops) or multiples (grows).
4. Debrief: what one question can you ask yourself to avoid grabbing the GCF by mistake?

strategy_links.why: Marcus's factor-list work is the exact swap error students make -- printed work makes it findable.
A number talk on 'how do you KNOW 12 is the least?' surfaces students who grab the product or the GCF.
Choral response on 'multiples GROW, factors FIT' builds the reflex that blocks the swap.

questioning_prompts: Is your answer in BOTH multiples rows? Point to it twice.
Can a least common multiple ever be smaller than the bigger of the two numbers? Why not?
You said 24 for 4 and 6 -- is 24 common? Is it the LEAST common? How do you check?
Which row is smarter to walk down, the 4s or the 6s? Why?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student answers with a small number like the GCF (2 for the LCM of 6 and 8) -- factor-thinking on a multiples question.
misconception_redirects.say: Put your finger on your answer. Find it in the multiples of 6 list. Now find it in the multiples of 8 list. A least common MULTIPLE must sit in both lists -- and it can never be smaller than the bigger starting number.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the first number both lists share -- that's exactly what least common multiple means.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the two numbers and answers the product every time (48 for 6 and 8).
misconception_redirects.say: The product is ALWAYS a common multiple, but is it the first one? Walk the 8s row: 8, 16, 24 -- check 24 against the 6s row before you jump to 48.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked for an earlier shared multiple -- that's the 'least' part of LCM.

quick_checks.prompt: Multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15. LCM -- go.
quick_checks.look_for: 10, fast. An answer of 1 or 2 means the GCF swap is live; 20 or beyond means they're not scanning from the start.

quick_checks.prompt: True or false: the LCM of 6 and 8 could be 4.
quick_checks.look_for: False, because 4 is smaller than 8 and multiples grow. Hesitation means the size anchor isn't set.

worked_solution.stem: Some multiples of 5 and 9 are listed. What is the least common multiple of 5 and 9?

steps.annotation: Both skip-counting rows are given. We want the FIRST number they share.

steps.math: Walk the 9s row: 9? no. 18? no. 27? no. 36? no. 45? YES
steps.annotation: Check each multiple of 9 against the 5s row -- walking the faster-growing row saves steps.
45 is in both rows, and nothing earlier is. Check: 45 / 5 = 9 and 45 / 9 = 5.

faded_example.stem: Some multiples of 4 and 6 are listed. What is the LCM of 4 and 6?

steps.annotation: Read both rows -- they grow forever, but we only need the start.

steps.math: Walk the 6s row: 6? not in the 4s. 12? YES -- 12 is in both rows.
steps.annotation: Check each multiple of 6 against the 4s row, starting from the smallest.
Name the first shared number -- not the product 24, which comes later.

The LCM can't be ___ because it is smaller than ___.

skills.name: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers to 100
skills.i_do_script: No lists this time -- we build them. Find the GCF of 15 and 20 with me. Factors of 15: I hunt in pairs -- 1 x 15, 3 x 5 -- so 1, 3, 5, 15. Factors of 20: 1 x 20, 2 x 10, 4 x 5 -- so 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. Common factors: 1 and 5. The GCF is 5. Say the question back before you start: greatest common FACTOR means factor lists, which STOP -- if you catch yourself skip-counting upward, you've wandered into LCM territory.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps GCF and LCM -- lists multiples instead of factors and reports the first shared multiple as the 'GCF'
canonical_error.example: Asked for the GCF of 6 and 8, the student writes 6, 12, 18, 24 and 8, 16, 24, then answers 24
canonical_error.why: Both routines are 'list numbers, find the shared one.' Without anchoring which direction each list runs (factors fit inside, multiples grow past), the student launches the more familiar skip-counting routine no matter which question was asked.

redirect_script.stop: Pause -- which word is in the question, factor or multiple?
redirect_script.prompt: Underline the word 'factor' in the question. Factors of 6 must fit INSIDE 6 -- can 24 fit inside 6? Rebuild your lists going DOWN: what divides 6? What divides 8?
redirect_script.praise: You matched the word to the right list -- factors that fit inside, then the greatest shared one.

skills.item_template: Find the GCF of two whole numbers (pairs <= 100, medium tier <= 50). Numeric response, no lists given. Student generates factor pairs for both numbers, identifies common factors, selects the greatest.

sample_items.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 15 and 20?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 60 (the LCM -- swap error), 1 (stopped at the first common factor), 300 (the product)

sample_items.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 28 and 84?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students rarely believe the GCF can be one of the numbers itself; 4 or 14 come from incomplete factor lists

sample_items.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 48?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 6 comes from missing the 12 x 3 / 12 x 4 pair; 144 is the LCM (swap error)

sample_items.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 42 and 70?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 7 or 2 come from stopping at an easy common factor without checking 14; 210 is the LCM

sample_items.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 27 and 45?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3 comes from stopping early; 135 is the LCM (swap error)

vocabulary.definition: The biggest number that divides evenly into both numbers.
Two numbers that multiply to the target, like 4 x 5 for 20 -- hunting in pairs keeps the list complete.
The first shared skip-counting number -- the OTHER tool; know it so you don't grab it by mistake.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'What is the greatest common factor of 15 and 20?' Underline the word 'factor.'
Factor or multiple -- which lists are we building, the kind that stop or the kind that grow forever?
Let's hunt factors of 15 in pairs. 1 times what makes 15? Does 2 work? 3 times what? Keep going -- when can we stop?
Record: Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. Then hunt 20 together: 1 x 20, 2 x 10, 4 x 5. Factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20.
Which numbers are in both lists? And of those, which is greatest?
If the student starts writing 15, 30, 45 or 20, 40, 60, stop them: 'Those lists are growing -- is that factors or multiples?' Let them name the swap themselves.
GCF of 15 and 20 is 5. The pair-hunting keeps your factor list complete -- most wrong GCFs come from a missing factor, not a wrong idea.
Your turn from scratch: find the GCF of 36 and 48. Talk me through your factor pairs as you go.

practice_problems.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 10 and 25?
What is the greatest common factor of 12 and 16?
What is the greatest common factor of 24 and 60?
practice_problems.notes: 6 is the common early exit -- push for complete factor lists.

practice_problems.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 32 and 48?
Jayla was asked to find the greatest common factor of 6 and 9. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Jayla: 'The first number in both lists is 18, so the answer is 18.'
practice_problems.answer: GCF = 3. Jayla listed MULTIPLES and found the least common multiple (18). The question asked for the greatest common FACTOR. Factors of 6: 1, 2, 3, 6. Factors of 9: 1, 3, 9. The greatest common factor is 3 -- and a factor of 6 can never be bigger than 6.
practice_problems.notes: The classic GCF-vs-LCM swap, baited with growing lists.

practice_problems.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 54 and 90?
practice_problems.notes: Bigger pair -- 6 and 9 are tempting early exits; only complete lists reach 18.

practice_problems.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 51 and 68?
practice_problems.notes: Unfriendly numbers: 51 = 3 x 17 and 68 = 4 x 17. Students who declare 'no common factors' need the pair hunt.

practice_problems.stem: Find two different pairs of numbers between 20 and 100 whose GCF is exactly 7. Prove each with factor lists.
practice_problems.answer: Example: 21 and 35 (GCF 7); 49 and 84 (GCF 7). Any pair of multiples of 7 whose quotients share no factor works.
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own reverses the direction.

activities.title: Which Tool Did Jayla Grab?
activities.instructions:
1. Partners read Jayla's work and decide: did she answer the question that was asked?
2. One partner rewrites the solution with FACTOR lists; the other checks that 18 can't be a factor of 6.
3. Debrief: what one-word check ('factor or multiple?') would have saved Jayla?

content.worked_problem: Find the GCF of 6 and 9. Jayla wrote: 6, 12, 18, 24, ... and 9, 18, 27, ... 'The first number in both lists is 18, so the answer is 18.'
content.error_step: Jayla listed multiples (skip-counting up) instead of factors (numbers that divide in), so she computed the LCM.
content.why: A factor of 6 must fit inside 6 -- it can never be 18. Factors of 6: 1, 2, 3, 6. Factors of 9: 1, 3, 9. GCF = 3.

activities.title: Factor Pair Rainbow Race
materials: Two dice-drawn or teacher-chosen numbers per round (like 36 & 48, 24 & 60, 42 & 70)
activities.instructions:
1. Each partner takes one number and draws a factor rainbow: 1 pairs with the number, then test 2, 3, 4... connecting each factor pair with an arc.
2. When both rainbows are done, circle the shared factors across the two papers and star the greatest.
3. Trade papers and audit: is any factor pair missing from your partner's rainbow?
4. Debrief: where do missing factors hide (usually the middle pairs like 6 x 8)?

activities.title: GCF or LCM? Say the Word First
materials: Question cards mixing GCF and LCM prompts
activities.instructions:
1. Flip a card and read it aloud. Before anyone computes, every student writes F (factors -- lists stop) or M (multiples -- lists grow) on their whiteboard and shows it.
2. Only after the letters agree does the group compute the answer.
3. One point for the right letter, one for the right number.
4. Debrief: which card almost tricked you into the wrong list?

strategy_links.why: The GCF-vs-LCM swap is this skill's signature failure -- students need reps spotting it in worked examples.
Gradual release fits the pair-hunting routine: model one complete factor rainbow, build one together, then release.
A think-aloud makes the invisible decision audible: 'factor means the lists stop, so I hunt pairs downward.'

questioning_prompts: Before you write anything: does this question say factor or multiple? What does that word make your lists do?
How do you KNOW your factor list for 36 is complete? Show me the pairs.
Could the GCF of 28 and 84 really be 28 -- one of the numbers itself? When does that happen?
Your answer is bigger than both numbers. What does that tell you about which list you built?
Is there a common factor bigger than the one you found? How would you check?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes growing lists (6, 12, 18...) for a GCF question and answers with the LCM.
misconception_redirects.say: Underline the word 'factor' in the question. Factors of 6 must fit INSIDE 6 -- can 24 fit inside 6? Rebuild your lists going DOWN: what divides 6? What divides 8?
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the word to the right list -- factors that fit inside, then the greatest shared one.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student stops at an early common factor (answers 6 for 36 and 48) because a middle factor pair is missing.
misconception_redirects.say: Hunt in pairs so nothing hides: 1 x 36, 2 x 18, 3 x 12, 4 x 9, 6 x 6. Now do 48 the same way and compare again.
misconception_redirects.praise: Complete pairs, complete list -- that's how you caught the 12.

quick_checks.prompt: GCF of 20 and 30 -- go. Then tell me one factor pair you used.
quick_checks.look_for: 10 with pairs like 2 x 10 or 5 x 6. An answer of 60 is the LCM swap; 5 means an incomplete list (missed 10).

quick_checks.prompt: I'm about to find the GCF of 8 and 12. Should my lists grow past 12 or stop at 12?
quick_checks.look_for: Stop -- factors fit inside. 'Grow' means the swap is still live before any arithmetic happens.

worked_solution.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 48?

steps.annotation: Hunt in pairs so nothing is missed: 1 x 36, 2 x 18, 3 x 12, 4 x 9, 6 x 6.
Same pair hunt: 1 x 48, 2 x 24, 3 x 16, 4 x 12, 6 x 8.
Circle the numbers that appear in BOTH lists.
Take the greatest circled number. Check: 36 / 12 = 3 and 48 / 12 = 4.

faded_example.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 24 and 60?

steps.annotation: Pair hunt: 1 x 24, 2 x 12, 3 x 8, 4 x 6.
Circle what appears in both lists.
Greatest of the circled numbers -- did you check past 6?

sentence_starters: The question says ___, so my lists should (stop / grow) and I will hunt factor pairs.
I know my factor list is complete because every pair from 1 x ___ up is checked.

skills.name: Find the least common multiple of two whole numbers to 12
skills.i_do_script: Now we build the multiples lists ourselves. Find the LCM of 8 and 12 with me. I skip-count the bigger number first: 12, 24, 36... and after each one I ask 'is that a multiple of 8?' 12? No. 24? Yes -- 8 x 3 = 24. Done: the LCM of 8 and 12 is 24. Notice I did NOT multiply 8 x 12 = 96. The product is always A common multiple, but it's usually not the LEAST one.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the two numbers and reports the product as the LCM without checking for an earlier common multiple
canonical_error.example: For the LCM of 8 and 12, the student answers 96 because 8 x 12 = 96
canonical_error.why: Multiplying always produces a common multiple, so the shortcut 'works' whenever the numbers share no factor (like 5 and 9) -- and the student generalizes it. They miss that any shared factor makes the true LCM smaller than the product.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- is there an earlier meeting point?
redirect_script.prompt: 96 IS a common multiple -- but is it the first one? Skip-count the 12s and check each against the 8s: 12, 24... stop the moment one is also a multiple of 8.
redirect_script.praise: You checked for an earlier shared multiple instead of trusting the product -- that's the 'least' in LCM.

skills.item_template: Find the LCM of two whole numbers <= 12 (difficult tier includes 7, 8, 12). Numeric response, no lists given. Student skip-counts the larger number, checking each multiple against the smaller.

sample_items.stem: What is the least common multiple of 7 and 12?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 (GCF swap), 19 (added instead), 168 (doubled the product); here the product IS the LCM since 7 and 12 share no factor

sample_items.stem: What is the least common multiple of 8 and 12?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 96 is the product shortcut; 4 is the GCF (swap error); 48 is a later common multiple

sample_items.stem: What is the least common multiple of 6 and 8?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 48 is the product shortcut; 2 is the GCF (swap error)

sample_items.stem: What is the least common multiple of 9 and 12?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 108 is the product shortcut; 3 is the GCF (swap error)

sample_items.stem: What is the least common multiple of 7 and 8?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 (GCF swap), 15 (added); with no shared factor the product is correct -- students need to know WHEN the shortcut works

vocabulary.definition: The first number that appears in both skip-counting lists.
The result of multiplying the two numbers -- always a common multiple, but often not the least one.
Counting by a number: 12, 24, 36, ... builds the multiples of 12.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'What is the least common multiple of 8 and 12?'
A lot of people would just do 8 x 12 = 96. Is 96 a common multiple of 8 and 12? How do you know?
But is 96 the LEAST common multiple? How could we check whether the lists meet earlier?
Skip-count the 12s on the board: 12, 24, 36. After each, test it against the 8s.
Is 12 a multiple of 8? Is 24? What times 8 gives 24?
24 is in both lists -- 12 x 2 and 8 x 3 -- so LCM(8, 12) = 24. The product 96 was a common multiple, just not the first one.
Watch for students who answer with the GCF (4). Ask: 'Is 4 in the 12s skip-count? Can a multiple of 12 be smaller than 12?'
Now you try two: LCM of 6 and 8, then LCM of 7 and 12. For the second one, tell me why the product turns out to be the answer.

practice_problems.stem: What is the least common multiple of 2 and 5?
What is the least common multiple of 3 and 4?
What is the least common multiple of 6 and 9?
practice_problems.notes: 54 (the product) is the bait -- the lists meet at 18.

practice_problems.stem: What is the least common multiple of 8 and 10?
practice_problems.notes: 80 (product) and 2 (GCF swap) are the expected misses.

practice_problems.stem: Leo found the least common multiple of 6 and 12. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Leo: 'To find the LCM you multiply the numbers, so the LCM of 6 and 12 is 72.'
practice_problems.answer: LCM = 12. Multiplying always gives A common multiple, but not always the least one. Skip-count the 12s: 12 -- and 12 is already a multiple of 6 (6 x 2). The lists meet at 12, far before 72.
practice_problems.notes: The product shortcut at its most extreme -- one number is a multiple of the other.

practice_problems.stem: What is the least common multiple of 10 and 12?
practice_problems.notes: 120 (product) is the bait; 2 (GCF) is the swap.

practice_problems.stem: What is the least common multiple of 11 and 12? Why does multiplying work for THIS pair?
practice_problems.answer: 132. Because 11 and 12 share no common factor except 1, the lists can't meet before the product.
practice_problems.notes: Names the condition under which the shortcut is legal.

practice_problems.stem: For which pairs does LCM = the product? Test 4 and 9, then 4 and 10, and explain the difference.
practice_problems.answer: LCM(4, 9) = 36 = 4 x 9 because 4 and 9 share no factor. LCM(4, 10) = 20, not 40, because 4 and 10 share the factor 2. The product rule only works when the GCF is 1.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch connecting GCF and LCM.

activities.title: Two-Color Clothesline
materials: A number line to 60 on the board or on register tape
Two colors of sticky dots or markers
activities.instructions:
1. Assign the pair 6 and 8. One student marks every multiple of 6 in one color; another marks every multiple of 8 in the second color.
2. The group calls out the first number wearing BOTH colors. That's the LCM.
3. Ask: where do the colors land together next (48)? What do you notice about 24, 48, ...?
4. Debrief: why did the colors meet before 6 x 8 = 48... wait, they DID meet at 24. What does that say about the multiply shortcut?

activities.title: Shortcut Legal or Illegal?
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows a pair of numbers, like '6 and 8' or '5 and 9.'
2. Partners sort: 'multiply shortcut WORKS (LCM = product)' vs 'shortcut FAILS (LCM is smaller).'
3. They must verify two cards from each pile by skip-counting.
4. Debrief: what do all the shortcut-works pairs have in common? (GCF is 1.)

activities.title: First to the Meeting Point
activities.instructions:
1. Flip a card. Both partners race to find the LCM -- but the answer only counts if they can SAY the check: '__ x __ = LCM both ways.'
2. An answer equal to the product when a smaller one exists scores minus one -- the shortcut trap card.
3. First to 5 points wins.
4. Debrief: which pair fooled you, and what was the earlier meeting point?

strategy_links.why: A number talk on 'LCM of 8 and 12 -- how did you get it?' surfaces the product shortcut publicly where it can be tested.
Leo's 72 is a one-line error students love to catch -- and catching it teaches when multiplying is and isn't legal.
The two-color number line is the concrete stage for LCM: students literally SEE the lists meet before the product.

questioning_prompts: You multiplied the two numbers. Is that always a common multiple? Is it always the LEAST one?
Which number's skip-count is smarter to walk, the 8s or the 12s? Why?
How do you know 24 is a multiple of BOTH 8 and 12? Say both facts.
When is the LCM of two numbers just the bigger number? Give me a pair.
For 7 and 12 the product IS the answer. What's special about 7 and 12?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the two numbers and reports the product as the LCM (96 for 8 and 12).
misconception_redirects.say: 96 IS a common multiple -- but is it the first one? Skip-count the 12s and check each against the 8s: 12, 24... stop the moment one is also a multiple of 8.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked for an earlier shared multiple instead of trusting the product -- that's the 'least' in LCM.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student answers with the GCF (4 for the LCM of 8 and 12) -- the swap in the other direction.
misconception_redirects.say: The question says MULTIPLE -- your answer has to be in the 12s skip-count. Can 4 be in a list that starts at 12 and grows?
misconception_redirects.praise: Right -- multiples grow, so the LCM is never smaller than the bigger number.

quick_checks.look_for: 12, instantly. 72 means the product shortcut is live; 6 means the size anchor (LCM >= bigger number) is missing.

quick_checks.prompt: Thumbs up or down: the LCM of two numbers is always their product.
quick_checks.look_for: Down, with a counterexample like 6 and 8 --> 24. A thumbs-up needs the two-color number line again.

worked_solution.stem: What is the least common multiple of 8 and 12?

steps.annotation: Walk the 12s -- the faster-growing list -- and test each one.

steps.math: 12: is it a multiple of 8? No. 24: 8 x 3 = 24 -- yes!
steps.annotation: Stop at the FIRST multiple of 12 that 8 also divides.
Check both directions: 12 x 2 = 24 and 8 x 3 = 24.

steps.math: Compare: 8 x 12 = 96 is a common multiple, but not the least
steps.annotation: The product shortcut overshoots whenever the numbers share a factor -- here they share 4.

faded_example.stem: What is the least common multiple of 6 and 9?

steps.annotation: Walk the bigger number's list.
Test each 9s number against the 6s until one hits.
Say both checks: 9 x 2 = 18 and 6 x 3 = 18. Not 54 -- that's the product.

sentence_starters: I skip-counted the ___s and the first one that ___ also divides is ___.
The product ___ is a common multiple, but the lists meet earlier at ___.

skills.name: Use the distributive property to rewrite a sum using the GCF
skills.i_do_script: We're going to pull a common factor OUT of a sum. Take 8 + 20. The GCF of 8 and 20 is 4. Now I rewrite EACH addend using that 4: 8 = 4 x 2 and 20 = 4 x 5. So 8 + 20 = 4(2 + 5). Both addends got divided by 4 -- that's the part students skip. Check it: 4 x 2 = 8, 4 x 5 = 20, and 4 x 7 = 28 = 8 + 20. The numbers inside the parentheses, 2 and 5, share no common factor -- that's how you know you pulled out the GREATEST common factor.

canonical_error.pattern: Factors the GCF out of only ONE addend and copies the other addend unchanged inside the parentheses
canonical_error.example: For 24 + 36, the student writes 12(2 + 36) instead of 12(2 + 3)
canonical_error.why: The student treats the distributive property as a notation move on the first number instead of dividing BOTH addends by the common factor. They never multiply back to check, so 12 x 38 = 456 slips past as '24 + 36.'

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- multiply it back out and see what you get.
redirect_script.prompt: Distribute your answer: what is 12 x 2? What is 12 x 36? Does 24 + 432 match 24 + 36? The GCF has to come out of BOTH addends -- divide the second number by 12 too.
redirect_script.praise: You divided both addends and your multiply-back check landed exactly on the original sum.

skills.item_template: Rewrite a sum of two whole numbers (sum <= 100, factors <= 12) as GCF(reduced + reduced), or find the missing value in an equation like 30 + 12 = 6(5 + __). Numeric or expression response; the numbers inside the parentheses must share no common factor.

sample_items.stem: An equation is shown. 30 + 12 = 6(5 + __). What number is missing from the equation?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12 is the addend copied unchanged (forgot to divide by 6); 6 is the GCF itself; 7 is 5 + 2, the finished sum inside

sample_items.stem: Use the distributive property and the greatest common factor of the two numbers to write an expression equivalent to 8 + 20.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4(2 + 20) forgets to divide the second addend; 2(4 + 10) uses a common factor that isn't greatest; 4(2 x 5) swaps + for x inside

sample_items.stem: Use the distributive property and the greatest common factor of the two numbers to write an expression equivalent to 36 + 8.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4(9 + 8) forgets the second addend; 2(18 + 4) factors out 2, which is common but not greatest

sample_items.stem: Use the distributive property and the greatest common factor of the two numbers to write an expression equivalent to 24 + 36.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12(2 + 36) forgets the second addend; 6(4 + 6) is not the GCF -- 4 and 6 still share a factor

sample_items.stem: Use the distributive property and the greatest common factor of the two numbers to write an expression equivalent to 27 + 45.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9(3 + 45) forgets the second addend; 3(9 + 15) uses 3, which is common but not greatest

vocabulary.definition: Multiplying a sum by a number is the same as multiplying each addend: 4(2 + 5) = 4 x 2 + 4 x 5.
A math phrase made of numbers and operations, like 4(2 + 5) -- no equals sign.
A statement that two expressions are equal, like 30 + 12 = 6(5 + 2).
The biggest number that divides both addends -- the number you pull out front.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 8 + 20. Say: 'We're going to rewrite this sum as a multiplication problem times a smaller sum.'
First job: what is the GCF of 8 and 20? Hunt the factor pairs if you need to.
Now rewrite each addend using that 4: 8 equals 4 times what? 20 equals 4 times what?
Write it as a stack: 8 + 20 = (4 x 2) + (4 x 5) = 4(2 + 5).
Both addends gave up a 4 -- what would go wrong if only the 8 did? What would 4(2 + 20) actually equal?
If the student writes 4(2 + 20), don't correct it -- have them distribute: 4 x 2 + 4 x 20 = 8 + 80. Let the 80 show them the 20 never got divided.
Look inside the parentheses: 2 and 5. Do they share any common factor? What does that tell you about the 4 we pulled out?
Your turn: rewrite 24 + 36 using its GCF, then multiply back to prove your expression equals 60.

practice_problems.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 6 and 15?
practice_problems.notes: The setup step -- every distributive rewrite starts here.

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the missing number: 6 + 10 = 2(3 + __).
Use the distributive property and the GCF to write an expression equivalent to 12 + 18.
practice_problems.notes: Multiply-back check: 6 x 2 = 12, 6 x 3 = 18.

practice_problems.stem: Use the distributive property and the GCF to write an expression equivalent to 9 + 21.
Priya used the distributive property to rewrite 16 + 40. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 16 + 40 = 8(2 + 5). Priya divided 16 by the GCF but copied 40 unchanged. The 8 must come out of BOTH addends: 40 = 8 x 5. Check: 8(2 + 5) = 8 x 7 = 56 = 16 + 40, while 8(2 + 40) = 336.
practice_problems.notes: The 'distributed but forgot one addend' error, baited with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: Use the distributive property and the GCF to write an expression equivalent to 40 + 48.
practice_problems.notes: 4(10 + 12) is the not-greatest trap -- 10 and 12 still share a 2.

practice_problems.stem: Go the other direction: expand 7(4 + 5) into a sum of two whole numbers that have a common factor of 7.
practice_problems.notes: Reversing direction proves the equivalence is owned, not memorized.

practice_problems.stem: Mia rewrote 24 + 32 as 4(6 + 8). Her expression is EQUAL to 24 + 32, but the teacher says she isn't done. Why not, and what is the finished answer?
practice_problems.answer: 6 and 8 still share a common factor of 2, so 4 is not the GREATEST common factor. Finished: 8(3 + 4).
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch -- the 'no common factor inside' test from the standard's own wording.

activities.title: The Forgotten Addend
activities.instructions:
1. Students read Priya's work and multiply her answer back out: 8 x 2 + 8 x 40.
2. They write the number her expression REALLY equals, then fix the expression.
3. Debrief question: what quick check catches this error every single time? (Distribute and compare.)

content.worked_problem: Rewrite 16 + 40 using the GCF. Priya wrote: GCF is 8; 16 = 8 x 2; so 16 + 40 = 8(2 + 40).
content.error_step: Priya factored the 8 out of 16 but copied 40 into the parentheses unchanged.
content.why: The GCF must divide BOTH addends: 40 = 8 x 5, so 16 + 40 = 8(2 + 5). Her version equals 8 x 42 = 336, not 56.

activities.title: Sum-Expression Match-Up
materials: Sum cards and expression cards, including two forgot-an-addend decoys
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up.
2. Match each sum to its GCF expression. Two expression cards are decoys that match nothing.
3. Every match must be proven with the multiply-back check, said aloud: '__ times __ plus __ times __ equals...'
4. Debrief: what made the decoys wrong -- and how fast did the multiply-back check expose them?

activities.title: Build It with Tiles
activities.instructions:
1. Build 8 + 20 as two separate tile rectangles: a 1-by-8 strip and a 1-by-20 strip.
2. Challenge: re-form BOTH strips into rectangles with the same height. What heights work? (1, 2, 4.)
3. With height 4, the strips become 4-by-2 and 4-by-5 -- push them together into one 4-by-7 rectangle. Write what you built: 4(2 + 5).
4. Debrief: why couldn't we use height 8? (8 doesn't divide 20 -- the GCF must fit BOTH addends.)

strategy_links.why: Pairing a correct worked rewrite next to the forgot-an-addend version makes the both-addends rule visible by contrast.
Tile rectangles make 'pulling out the GCF' physical -- both strips must be re-formed to the same height before they can join.
Whiteboard Pass on one rewrite shows instantly who is copying the second addend unchanged.

questioning_prompts: Before anything else: what is the GCF of the two addends, and how do you know it's the greatest?
Multiply your expression back out. Does it land exactly on the original sum?
Look inside your parentheses. Do those two numbers share a common factor? What should be true?
In 30 + 12 = 6(5 + __), where did the 5 come from? So where must the blank come from?
What's the difference between what 4(2 + 20) equals and what 8 + 20 equals? Which addend never paid its 4?

misconception_redirects.say: Distribute your answer: what is 12 x 2? What is 12 x 36? Does 24 + 432 match 24 + 36? The GCF has to come out of BOTH addends -- divide the second number by 12 too.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided both addends and your multiply-back check landed exactly on the original sum.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student pulls out a common factor that isn't the greatest -- writes 2(4 + 10) for 8 + 20.
misconception_redirects.say: Your expression is equal -- nice -- but look inside: 4 and 10 still share a 2. Pull the FULL greatest common factor out front so the inside pair shares nothing.
misconception_redirects.praise: Now the numbers inside share no common factor -- that's the proof you found the GCF.

quick_checks.prompt: Fill the blank in 10 + 25 = 5(2 + __) and prove it in one line.
quick_checks.look_for: 5, with the check 5 x 5 = 25. An answer of 25 is the forgot-to-divide error; 7 means they added 2 + 5 instead.

quick_checks.prompt: Is 6(2 + 3) equivalent to 12 + 18? Show me without saying 'yes.'
quick_checks.look_for: Distributing: 6 x 2 = 12 and 6 x 3 = 18. Students who just re-add 12 + 18 = 30 and 6 x 5 = 30 are fine too -- both checks are valid.

worked_solution.stem: Use the distributive property and the GCF to write an expression equivalent to 24 + 36.

steps.annotation: Find the greatest common factor of BOTH addends first.
Divide each addend by the GCF -- both addends, not just the first.
The GCF goes out front; the leftover pieces go inside. 2 and 3 share no common factor -- proof we used the GREATEST factor.
Multiply back out. If it doesn't land on the original sum, an addend never got divided.

skills.name: Solve real-world problems by choosing GCF or LCM
skills.i_do_script: Real problems never say 'GCF' or 'LCM' -- the story tells you which tool to grab. Listen: 'Karl goes to the beach every 7 days, Annie every 3 days. When will they be there together?' Things repeating on schedules until they LINE UP -- that's multiples, so LCM: 21 days. Different story: 'Sara has 16 red flowers and 24 yellow and wants identical bouquets.' Splitting two amounts into equal groups -- that's dividing, so GCF: 8 bouquets. Ask yourself: are the numbers growing until they meet, or being broken into groups?

canonical_error.pattern: Grabs the wrong tool for the story -- computes the GCF for a things-lining-up problem or the LCM for an equal-groups problem
canonical_error.example: For 'buses every 6 and 8 minutes -- when do they arrive together?', the student finds the GCF and answers 2 minutes
canonical_error.why: The student pattern-matches 'two numbers, common something' without asking what the story is doing. Schedules repeat and grow (multiples); sharing splits downward (factors). Without that anchor, whichever routine was practiced last wins.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- what is the story actually doing?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask the size question: should the answer be BIGGER than 6 and 8 (waiting for schedules to line up) or SMALLER (cutting into groups)? Buses keep coming -- the meeting time grows. Which list grows: factors or multiples?
redirect_script.praise: You read the story first and picked the tool second -- that's exactly the right order.

skills.item_template: A short real-world scenario (numbers within GCF <= 100 / LCM <= 12 limits): repeating schedules that align (LCM) or two quantities split into greatest equal groups (GCF). Numeric response with unit.

sample_items.stem: Last summer, Karl and Annie went to the beach. Karl went to the beach every 7 days. Annie went to the beach every 3 days. They were both at the beach today. How many days will pass until they see each other at the beach again?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 (GCF -- swap error), 10 (added 7 + 3), 42 (doubled the LCM or used 6 x 7)

sample_items.stem: Sara is making bouquets of flowers. She has 16 red flowers and 24 yellow flowers. She wants every bouquet to be identical, using all the flowers. What is the greatest number of bouquets Sara can make?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 48 (LCM -- swap error), 4 (a common factor but not greatest), 40 (added the amounts)

sample_items.stem: Bus A arrives at the station every 6 minutes. Bus B arrives every 10 minutes. Both buses just arrived together. In how many minutes will both buses arrive together again?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 (GCF -- swap error), 16 (added), 60 (the product -- missed the earlier meeting at 30)

sample_items.stem: A teacher has 36 granola bars and 48 juice boxes for a field trip. She wants to make identical snack packs with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of snack packs she can make?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 144 (LCM -- swap error), 6 (a common factor but not greatest), 84 (added the amounts)

vocabulary.definition: The tool for SPLITTING two amounts into the largest possible identical groups.
The tool for finding when repeating events LINE UP again.
Groups that all contain exactly the same amounts -- the signal phrase for GCF stories.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.NS.5 -- applying properties of operations with rational numbers.

worked_example_script.text: Write the two stories side by side: the beach story (every 7 days / every 3 days) and the bouquet story (16 red / 24 yellow, identical bouquets).
Neither story says GCF or LCM. Read the beach story -- what is happening to the days as we wait? Growing or splitting?
So which list matches days that keep coming -- factors that stop, or multiples that grow?
Solve it: multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21. Circle 21 in both.
Now the bouquet story: is anything repeating on a schedule? Or are we cutting 16 and 24 into groups?
Groups means dividing -- so which tool? What is the GCF of 16 and 24?
If the student computes the LCM (48 bouquets), ask: 'Sara only has 16 red flowers. Can she make 48 identical bouquets?' Let the story's own size logic expose the swap.
Two questions crack every story: Is something repeating until it lines up? LCM. Are we splitting amounts into identical groups? GCF. And the answer's SIZE tells you if you grabbed the wrong one.

practice_problems.stem: Hot dogs come in packs of 8 and buns come in packs of 6. What is the smallest number of hot dogs and buns you can buy to have exactly the same number of each?
Deja has 12 pencils and 18 erasers. She wants to make identical gift bags with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of gift bags she can make?
practice_problems.answer: 6 gift bags

practice_problems.stem: One lighthouse flashes every 4 seconds. Another flashes every 10 seconds. They just flashed together. In how many seconds will they flash together again?
practice_problems.answer: 20 seconds
practice_problems.notes: 2 (GCF swap) and 40 (product) are the expected misses.

practice_problems.stem: A florist has 30 carnations and 42 roses. She wants to make identical bouquets using every flower. What is the greatest number of bouquets she can make?
practice_problems.answer: 6 bouquets
practice_problems.notes: 2 or 3 mean an incomplete factor hunt; 210 means the swap.

practice_problems.stem: Amir solved this problem: 'One runner does a lap every 6 minutes, another every 8 minutes. They start together. When will they cross the start line together again?' Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Amir: 'The greatest common factor is 2, so they meet again in 2 minutes.'
practice_problems.answer: 24 minutes. The laps REPEAT and grow -- that's multiples, not factors. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. They line up at 24. Amir's answer of 2 minutes fails the size test: neither runner has even finished one lap in 2 minutes.
practice_problems.notes: The GCF-vs-LCM swap inside a context -- the size test exposes it.

practice_problems.stem: Malik gets a haircut every 4 weeks. His brother gets one every 6 weeks. They both got haircuts this week. In how many weeks will they get haircuts in the same week again?
practice_problems.answer: 12 weeks
practice_problems.notes: 24 (the product) misses the earlier meeting at 12.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own story problem whose answer is the GCF of 20 and 30, then solve it.
practice_problems.answer: Example: 'A chef has 20 strawberries and 30 grapes and wants identical fruit cups with nothing left over. Greatest number of cups?' GCF(20, 30) = 10.
practice_problems.notes: Producing a story proves the student owns the meaning, not just the routine.

practice_problems.stem: Nia has 18 red beads and 27 blue beads. She makes the greatest possible number of identical bracelets with nothing left over. How many bracelets does she make, AND how many beads of each color are on one bracelet?
practice_problems.answer: 9 bracelets, each with 2 red beads and 3 blue beads.
practice_problems.notes: The follow-up division (18/9 and 27/9) is where the reduced pair from S5 quietly reappears.

activities.title: Two Minutes? Check the Size!
activities.instructions:
1. Read Amir's runner problem and his answer of 2 minutes aloud.
2. Groups answer: what does '2 minutes' claim happened? Could either runner even finish a lap?
3. Rebuild the solution with multiples lists and find the real answer.
4. Debrief: how does checking the SIZE of an answer against the story catch a tool swap instantly?

content.worked_problem: Runners lap every 6 and 8 minutes, starting together. Amir listed factors of 6 and 8, found the common factor 2, and answered '2 minutes.'
content.error_step: Amir used factor lists (GCF) on a story about laps repeating until they line up (LCM).
content.why: Repeating events need multiples: 6, 12, 18, 24 and 8, 16, 24 meet at 24 minutes. The answer 2 is smaller than either lap time -- impossible for a meeting time.

activities.title: Story Slam
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a pair card. Each student writes a 2-sentence story for that pair -- and secretly decides if it's a GCF story or an LCM story.
2. Read stories aloud; the group votes GCF or LCM before the author reveals.
3. Solve the winning (trickiest) story together.
4. Debrief: what did the trickiest story do to disguise its tool?

strategy_links.why: Tool-choice is a reasoning decision -- Think-Pair-Share lets students defend GCF vs LCM before any computation.
Amir's 2-minute answer is a swap error a whole group can dismantle with the size test.
Thinking aloud 'is this story growing until things meet, or splitting into groups?' models the exact internal question.

questioning_prompts: Before you compute: is the story WAITING for things to line up, or SPLITTING things into groups?
Should your answer be bigger than both numbers or smaller? What does the story say?
You answered 2 minutes -- can a bus that comes every 6 minutes arrive twice in 2 minutes?
What in the bouquet story told you to divide instead of skip-count?
Rewrite this LCM story so it becomes a GCF story. What did you have to change?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes the GCF for a schedules-lining-up story (answers 2 minutes for buses every 6 and 8 minutes).
misconception_redirects.say: Ask the size question: should the answer be BIGGER than 6 and 8 (waiting for schedules to line up) or SMALLER (cutting into groups)? Buses keep coming -- the meeting time grows. Which list grows: factors or multiples?
misconception_redirects.praise: You read the story first and picked the tool second -- that's exactly the right order.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes the LCM for an equal-groups story (answers 48 bouquets from 16 and 24 flowers).
misconception_redirects.say: Sara only HAS 16 red flowers -- can she make 48 identical bouquets? Splitting flowers into groups means dividing, and dividing means factors.
misconception_redirects.praise: You caught it with the story's own numbers -- an answer can't be bigger than what Sara is holding.

quick_checks.prompt: One word each: bells ringing every 4 and 6 minutes -- GCF or LCM? Cutting two ribbons into equal pieces -- GCF or LCM?
quick_checks.look_for: LCM then GCF, fast. Hesitation or a coin-flip pattern means the growing-vs-splitting anchor isn't set.

quick_checks.prompt: A student got 90 as the answer to 'greatest number of identical teams from 30 girls and 45 boys.' Without solving, how do you know 90 is wrong?
quick_checks.look_for: Size reasoning: you can't make more teams than there are people; the tool must be GCF (answer 15). Recomputing without size reasoning misses the point.

worked_solution.stem: Bus A arrives every 6 minutes and Bus B arrives every 10 minutes. Both just arrived together. In how many minutes will they arrive together again?

steps.math: Story check: buses KEEP COMING until their arrivals line up
steps.annotation: Repeating events that line up means multiples -- this is an LCM problem, and the answer must be bigger than 10.
Walk the bigger number's list and test each against the 6s.
30 is the first number in both lists: 10 x 3 and 6 x 5.
Size check: 30 is bigger than both 6 and 10 -- sensible for a meeting time. (The GCF, 2, would mean buses meeting before either even returns.)

faded_example.stem: A chef has 24 strawberries and 40 grapes. He makes the greatest possible number of identical fruit cups with nothing left over. How many fruit cups does he make?

steps.math: Story check: SPLITTING two amounts into identical groups --> GCF
steps.annotation: Nothing repeats or grows; we're dividing amounts into groups.
Hunt factor pairs for both amounts.
Greatest shared factor. Check the story: 24 / 8 = 3 strawberries and 40 / 8 = 5 grapes per cup.
